title: OAuth 2.0 & OIDC Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on OAuth 2.0 roles, the authorization code flow with PKCE, token types, scopes, OIDC discovery and claims, SAML vs OIDC for SSO, and the mistakes that cause real breaches.

chapters.title: OAuth Mental Model and Roles
points: OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: an app gets limited access to a user's resources without ever seeing their password
Four roles: Resource Owner (the user), Client (the app), Authorization Server (issues tokens), Resource Server (the API that accepts tokens)
Authentication vs authorization: OAuth answers 'what may this app do?'; OIDC adds 'who is the user?' on top of it
Public clients (SPA, mobile) cannot keep a secret; confidential clients (server-side) can and authenticate with client_id plus client_secret
Front channel = browser redirects (visible, untrusted); back channel = direct server-to-server calls (token endpoint, trusted)

chapters.title: Authorization Code Flow with PKCE
points: Step 1: client generates a random code_verifier (43-128 chars) and code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) with code_challenge_method=S256
Step 2: redirect to /authorize with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge
Step 3: user logs in and consents; the server redirects back to redirect_uri with ?code=...&state=...; client must check state matches
Step 4: back-channel POST to /token with grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier; the server hashes the verifier and compares it to the challenge

PKCE stops authorization code interception: a stolen code is useless without the verifier; use it for all clients, and it is mandatory for public clients; implicit flow is deprecated; client_credentials is for machine-to-machine with no user

chapters.title: Access, Refresh and ID Tokens
points: Access token: short-lived (minutes), sent as 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' to the resource server; audience is the API
ID token: an OIDC JWT proving who the user authenticated as; consumed by the client only, never sent to an API as a credential
Refresh token: long-lived, exchanged at /token with grant_type=refresh_token for a new access token; never sent to the resource server
Validate a JWT: check signature via the JWKS key (kid), then iss, aud, exp, and nonce for ID tokens; opaque tokens are validated through introspection (RFC 7662)
Refresh token rotation issues a new refresh token on each use and detects reuse of an old one; store tokens in httpOnly secure cookies or server-side, not localStorage

chapters.title: Scopes, OIDC Discovery and Claims
points: Scopes are the permissions a client requests, as space-separated strings (e.g. 'read:calendar write:calendar'); the user consents and the server may grant less than requested
OIDC adds the 'openid' scope (required to get an ID token); profile, email, address and phone scopes map to groups of claims
Standard ID token claims: iss (issuer), sub (stable unique user id), aud, exp, iat, nonce, plus email, name; key on sub, never on email

Discovery: GET {issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration returns authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, userinfo_endpoint, jwks_uri and supported scopes, so clients configure from the issuer URL alone
The /userinfo endpoint returns claims for a valid access token; the nonce parameter binds the ID token to the request and prevents replay

chapters.title: SSO: SAML vs OIDC and Common Mistakes
points: SAML 2.0: XML assertions signed with XML-DSig, POSTed through the browser to the SP's ACS URL; common in enterprise and legacy apps; roles are Identity Provider (IdP) and Service Provider (SP)
OIDC: JSON/JWT over HTTPS on top of OAuth 2.0; fits SPAs, mobile and APIs; easier to implement and the better default for new apps
SP-initiated SSO starts at the app, which redirects to the IdP; IdP-initiated starts at the IdP portal and is more exposed to CSRF and replay
Mistake: skipping or not verifying the state parameter, which allows CSRF login attacks
Mistake: loose redirect_uri matching; always register exact URIs, since open redirects leak codes and tokens
Mistake: using an access token as proof of login, or not validating aud and iss on tokens
Mistake: tokens in localStorage, long-lived access tokens, over-broad scopes, or a client_secret shipped in a SPA or mobile app

chapters.title: OAuth and OIDC Cheat Sheet
points: Endpoints: /authorize (front channel), /token (back channel), /userinfo, /jwks, /.well-known/openid-configuration
Flow picks: user plus browser app = authorization code + PKCE; machine-to-machine = client_credentials; avoid implicit and password grants
Token cheat: access token = call the API; ID token = who logged in; refresh token = get a new access token
Always send state (CSRF) and nonce (replay), validate iss, aud, exp and the signature, and use exact redirect_uri matching
SAML vs OIDC: SAML = XML for enterprise SSO; OIDC = JWT for modern web and mobile
